body_markdown:
How to choose among a PEO, an ASO and managed payroll
Choosing among a professional employer organization (PEO), an administrative services organization (ASO) and managed payroll comes down to who is the employer for federal employment taxes, under whose employer identification number (EIN) the returns are filed, and what stays with the employer. The IRS says an employer that outsources payroll and related tax duties to a third-party payer will generally remain responsible for those duties, including liability for the taxes, with an exception for certified professional employer organizations.
What decides liability when someone else handles payroll
The IRS says who is liable depends on the facts and the type of third-party arrangement, and that an employer may remain solely liable for federal employment taxes, may become jointly and severally liable, or may be relieved of liability. The IRS also says liability is set by the Internal Revenue Code and cannot be changed by a private agreement or contract. The label on a service, whether PEO, ASO or managed payroll, does not decide liability, so the facts of the arrangement do.
How the IRS sorts third-party payroll arrangements
The IRS compares four arrangements in its third party arrangement chart by the form filed with the IRS, the EIN used to file and who has employment tax liability. The four are the payroll service provider, the reporting agent, the section 3504 agent and the certified professional employer organization (CPEO).


The IRS describes a PEO as an organization that performs some or all of a client’s federal employment tax withholding, reporting and payment functions, and it may also manage human resources, employee benefits, workers compensation claims and unemployment insurance claims. A PEO is not required to be certified, and the IRS runs a voluntary certification program under which a certified PEO is a CPEO. Industry usage describes a PEO as a co-employment model, but the IRS says the Code does not define “co-employer” and the concept is not recognized under federal tax law.


ASO, short for administrative services organization, is an industry term for a provider that takes on full administrative outsourcing of payroll and HR work. The IRS and the Department of Labor do not define the term for payroll or HR, so the tax result follows the facts, namely who pays the wages, under whose EIN the returns are filed and whether the provider asserts it is the employer. In this guide, managed payroll means a provider’s specialists run payroll and day-to-day HR administration for the employer, and the IRS arrangement it falls under depends on the form filed and whose EIN files.


As of October 2026, the rows below follow the chart above, the IRS page for CPEO customers, section 3511 of the Internal Revenue Code, Treasury Regulation 31.3504-2, the IRS page on PEO arrangements and Internal Revenue Manual 5.1.24.


Arrangement
Who is the employer for federal employment taxes
Who files, and under whose EIN
What stays with the employer
Employer runs its own payroll
The common law employer
The employer, under its own EIN
All of it, because the employer is the responsible party
Payroll service provider or reporting agent
The employer, because the IRS chart says neither a payroll service provider nor a reporting agent has employment tax liability
A payroll service provider prepares returns using the employer’s EIN, and the employer signs them. A reporting agent signs and generally e-files returns using each client’s EIN
Responsibility for ensuring that returns are filed and deposits and payments are made on time
Section 3504 agent
The employer, and the agent is jointly liable
The agent files aggregate returns under the agent’s own EIN
Joint liability with the agent. The employer files its own Form 940 under its own EIN, with an exception for home care service recipients through a state or local program
PEO that is not a CPEO
In the arrangement the IRS describes, the client typically remains the common law employer. A PEO that meets the service-agreement definition in Treasury Regulation 31.3504-2 is designated to perform employer acts for the wages it pays, unless the wages are reported on a return filed under the client’s EIN
A PEO may file an aggregate Form 941 using the PEO’s EIN
The client remains subject to the law that applies to an employer, and the IRS says the PEO and the client are concurrently liable when the PEO is designated under the regulation
CPEO
The CPEO, for a worksite employee and only for pay the CPEO remits to that employee
The CPEO reports wages under the CPEO’s EIN and allocates them to each customer by the customer’s EIN on Schedule R. It files Forms W-2 and W-3 under its own EIN
Possible liability for pay the CPEO remits to non-worksite employees. Customers cannot view the CPEO’s deposits in EFTPS
ASO (the label)
Follows the facts, not the label. Does the provider assert that it is the employer, explicitly or implicitly?
Follows the facts. Under whose EIN will each return be filed?
Follows the facts, and no contract can change statutory liability. Which duties does the agreement leave with the employer?
Managed payroll (the label)
Depends on the arrangement. Which IRS form, if any, is on file for the business?
Under whose EIN will each return be filed?
Which duties will the provider perform, and which stay with the employer?
How to answer the questions that decide the choice
What you need first. Your employee count, the states where employees work, which employees are paid hourly, and who handles payroll and HR today.


1. Decide whether the business should stay the employer for federal employment taxes. Under the IRS common-law test, a business is the employer when it can control what work is done and how it is done, even if it gives the worker freedom of action. In a PEO arrangement, the IRS reviews whether the client directs the day-to-day duties, keeps the authority to hire and fire, and sets pay. Write down whether the business will keep doing those three things. The second column of the table shows how each arrangement answers the question.
2. Decide how much control of benefits plans, brokers and retirement partners the business wants to keep. Write down which of those choices must stay with the business.
3. Name who will run payroll and HR day to day. Write down the person or team that would own each pay cycle, each new hire and each change, and who covers when that person is out.
4. Count the states. The IRS says state PEO laws have no bearing on federal employment tax liability. List every state where employees work.
5. Mark the hourly workforce. List the employees paid hourly and where their time and overtime records are kept.
6. Mark the compliance exposure. List the compliance areas the business answers for, from payroll tax to hiring and benefits.


What a correct result looks like. The business has one written answer to each of the six questions, in a form it can hand to every provider it talks to.
Choosing between running payroll and HR yourself and having Asure’s experts manage it
Questions two, three and six set up one more choice, which is whether the business runs payroll and HR itself or has specialists do the work.


AsureCentral is built for growing employers that run payroll and HR themselves. AsureWorks is the managed service on the same platform. With AsureWorks, Asure specialists do the work on AsureCentral and the client remains the employer, with statutory liability staying with the employer, which matches the IRS’s general rule that an employer who outsources payroll duties will generally remain responsible for them. Asure is not a co-employment PEO.
What stays with the employer when someone else runs payroll
Generally, and with an exception for CPEOs, an employer that contracts with a third party remains responsible for ensuring that returns are filed and deposits and payments are made, and if the third party fails to make the deposits and payments, the IRS may assess penalties and interest on the employer’s account. For a PEO that is not a CPEO, the IRS says in its guidance to examiners that a client using a PEO generally is not relieved of its employment tax obligation for wages paid to its employees, and it directs examiners to advise the client to use due diligence in selecting and continuing with a PEO. The employer also keeps employment tax records for at least four years.
How to keep watch on your own IRS account
What you need first. The business’s EIN and the address the IRS holds for the business.


1. When a third party enrolls the business in EFTPS for federal tax deposits, activate the Inquiry PIN the business receives. The IRS says the employer should use it to monitor its account and ensure the third party is making the required tax deposits.
2. Keep the business’s own address as the address of record with the IRS, and use Form 8822-B to update it. The IRS strongly recommends this because it sends correspondence on account issues to that address, and mail sent to a third-party payer’s address may significantly limit the employer’s ability to be informed.
3. Where the business is eligible, use its own IRS Business Tax Account to view payment history and read IRS notices.


What a correct result looks like. The business holds its own IRS account access, receives IRS correspondence at its own address, and has a named person who reviews the account.
How to put the answers in writing before you sign
What you need first. The six written answers from earlier and each provider’s draft agreement.


1. Ask whether the provider is a CPEO and which exact legal name and EIN appear in the contract. The IRS says a CPEO contract must contain the CPEO’s exact name and EIN, and it publishes a list of certified CPEOs that it updates every calendar quarter, with separate lists of suspended and revoked CPEOs.
2. Ask which IRS forms will be on file for the business. Form 8655 is for a reporting agent, Form 2678 for a section 3504 agent and Form 8973 for a CPEO, and the chart lists none required for a payroll service provider.
3. Ask under whose EIN Forms 941, 940, W-2 and W-3 will be filed.
4. Ask whether the agreement has the provider assert, explicitly or implicitly, that it is the employer or co-employer, and whether the provider pays the wages and assumes responsibility for the taxes. Those are the three elements of a service agreement under Treasury Regulation 31.3504-2.
5. If the provider is a reporting agent, ask for its written statement. Revenue Procedure 2012-32 has a reporting agent give the client that statement when the contract starts and at least quarterly, saying the client remains responsible for timely filing and payment.
6. If the provider files aggregate returns, ask whether a Schedule R will be filed for the business, how wages will be allocated to the business’s EIN on it, and how the business will receive client-level reports.
7. Ask what notice the business will receive, and when, if a CPEO’s certification is suspended, revoked or ended. The IRS requires a CPEO to give customers written notice of a suspension or revocation, and the notice of a revocation must say that section 3511 no longer applies to the customer’s relationship with the CPEO and that the customer may also be liable.
8. Ask what the base fee covers, which HR and benefits services are in scope, the service levels, the implementation time and the fees on exit.


What a correct result looks like. Every answer appears in the signed agreement or in a schedule attached to it, in the provider’s own words, rather than in a sales conversation or on a web page.
Frequently asked questions
Does using a payroll provider change who is liable for payroll taxes?
It depends on the arrangement, and the IRS names the CPEO as the exception to the general rule that the employer remains responsible. The employer, not the provider, stays liable under a payroll service provider or a reporting agent. A section 3504 agent is liable along with the employer, and the IRS says a PEO that is not a CPEO and is designated under Treasury Regulation 31.3504-2 is concurrently liable with its client. A CPEO is generally solely liable for the taxes on pay it remits to worksite employees, and the IRS chart says a CPEO and its customer may both be liable for non-worksite employees.
Is an ASO the same as a PEO?
The IRS describes a PEO but does not define an ASO for payroll or HR, and it does not recognize “co-employer” as a status under federal tax law, so the label alone does not settle the question. Under Treasury Regulation 31.3504-2, the test is whether the provider asserts it is the employer or co-employer, pays the wages and assumes responsibility for the taxes, so describe any provider by those facts.
What is a certified professional employer organization, and how can I check one?
A CPEO is a PEO that applied to the IRS’s voluntary certification program and that the IRS has certified. Under section 3511, a CPEO is treated as the employer of a worksite employee for federal employment taxes, but only for pay it remits to that employee. To check one, find its exact legal name on the IRS list of certified CPEOs and confirm that the contract shows that exact name and the CPEO’s EIN.
Whose EIN is on the payroll tax returns?
It depends on the arrangement. A payroll service provider or reporting agent uses the employer’s EIN, a section 3504 agent files aggregate returns under its own EIN, a PEO that is not a CPEO may file an aggregate Form 941 using its own EIN, and a CPEO reports wages under its own EIN and allocates them to each customer by the customer’s EIN on Schedule R.
What should the employer still monitor when someone else handles payroll?
The employer keeps its own view of its IRS account. When a third party enrolls the business in EFTPS, the Inquiry PIN lets the business monitor that third party’s deposits, although a CPEO’s customers cannot view the deposits the CPEO makes in EFTPS. The IRS strongly recommends keeping the business’s own address as the address of record, and a Business Tax Account shows payment history and IRS notices.
